blocks.text: A public health laboratory receives a sachet of drinking water and must state exactly how much dissolved carbonate it contains. No instrument reads that off directly. A burette, a pipette and a few drops of indicator will, and the technique is one you can master in a single practical.

blocks.title: Titration terms
blocks.text: A standard solution is one whose concentration is accurately known. The end point is the moment the indicator changes colour permanently. The titre is the volume of solution delivered from the burette. Concordant titres are readings that agree within 0.10 cm3 of each other.

blocks.markdown:
## The apparatus and why each is used

- **Pipette** — delivers one fixed accurate volume, usually 20.0 or 25.0 cm3, into the conical flask. Fill using a pipette filler, never by mouth, and allow it to drain naturally without blowing out the last drop.
- **Burette** — delivers a variable, accurately measured volume. It is graduated in 0.10 cm3 divisions and read from the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
- **Conical flask** — its shape allows vigorous swirling without splashing.
- **White tile** — placed under the flask so the colour change stands out.

items: Rinse the burette with the solution it will contain and the pipette with the solution it will deliver, so residual water does not dilute them
Rinse the conical flask with distilled water only, because any solution left behind would add extra moles
Pipette 25.0 cm3 of the solution to be analysed into the conical flask and add two or three drops of indicator
Fill the burette above the zero mark, run the tip full to expel the air bubble, then take the initial reading
Titrate, swirling continuously, adding dropwise near the end point until one drop produces a permanent colour change
Record the final reading, repeat until two or three titres are concordant, and average only the concordant values

blocks.caption: The titration relationship; nA and nB are the coefficients of acid and base in the balanced equation

blocks.title: Finding an unknown concentration
blocks.prompt: 25.0 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution required 22.5 cm3 of 0.100 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid for complete neutralisation. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol/dm3 and in g/dm3. [Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1]

steps.text: Write the balanced equation: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. The mole ratio of acid to base is 1 : 1.
Find the moles of the substance you know completely, the acid.
Apply the mole ratio. Since HCl : NaOH is 1 : 1, moles of NaOH = 0.00225 mol.
Divide by the volume of base in dm3.
Convert to grams per cubic decimetre. M(NaOH) = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g/mol, so 0.0900 x 40 = 3.60 g/dm3.
Check the sense of the answer: less than 25 cm3 of acid neutralised 25 cm3 of base, so the base must be slightly more dilute than the acid. It is, at 0.09 against 0.10 mol/dm3.

blocks.title: Averaging burette readings
blocks.prompt: A student records the following titres: rough 25.00 cm3, first 24.20 cm3, second 24.30 cm3, third 24.90 cm3. Calculate the average titre to be used in the calculation.

steps.text: Discard the rough titration immediately. It is only there to locate the end point roughly and is always less accurate.
Look for concordant values, those within 0.10 cm3 of each other. The first and second titres, 24.20 and 24.30, differ by exactly 0.10 cm3, so they are concordant.
The third titre of 24.90 differs from both by more than 0.10 cm3, so it is discarded as an outlier, most likely from overshooting the end point.
Quote the answer to two decimal places, as burette readings always are.

blocks.title: Errors that shift the titre
blocks.text: An air bubble left in the burette tip that escapes during titration makes the titre too high. Rinsing the conical flask with the solution it will hold rather than with distilled water adds extra moles and also raises the titre. Rinsing the burette with distilled water and not with the titrant dilutes it, so more must be delivered and the titre again reads high.

points: A pipette delivers one fixed volume; a burette delivers a variable measured volume.
Rinse the burette and pipette with the solutions they will hold, but the conical flask with distilled water only.
Discard the rough titre and average only concordant values, those within 0.10 cm3.
Use CaVa / CbVb = na / nb with the coefficients from the balanced equation.
Convert cm3 to dm3 by dividing by 1000 before calculating moles.
